segments.english: Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years, and he fathered Lamech.
segments.literal: and-lived Methuselah seven and-eighty year and-hundred-of year and-he-fathered [object-marker] Lamech

tokens.note: Hifil wayyiqtol of ילד: 'caused to bear', 'begot'

phrases.literal: 'and-lived Methuselah'; the English puts the subject first
'seven and-eighty year and-hundred year': the Hebrew gives units, tens, then hundreds

grammar: The age is given units first: 'seven and eighty year and hundred year'; English reverses it to 'one hundred eighty-seven'.
וַיְחִי and וַיּוֹלֶד are wayyiqtols: the narrative chain of the genealogy.
The tevir on וּשְׁמֹנִים and tipḥa on שָׁנָה mark off the units and tens; the etnaḥta on the second שָׁנָה ends the first half of the verse.
segments.note: Fixed genealogical formula; the 'year' is repeated after the tens and after the hundreds.

commentary.summary: Onkelos renders the verse closely: Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years and begot Lamech; he reverses the order of the numbers as the English does.

segments.english: Methuselah lived, after he fathered Lamech, seven hundred eighty-two years, and he fathered sons and daughters.
segments.literal: and-lived Methuselah after fathering-him [object-marker] Lamech two and-eighty year and-seven hundreds year and-he-fathered sons and-daughters

tokens.note: Hifil infinitive construct with 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'his begetting'
feminine dual of שְׁנַיִם in construct-like form, agreeing with שָׁנָה

phrases.literal: 'after fathering-him Lamech': infinitive construct with suffix is a temporal clause

grammar: אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition plus infinitive construct with suffix: 'after his begetting', rendered as a clause.
The accents (pashta on אַחֲרֵי, zaqef on לֶמֶךְ) set the 'after' clause apart before the number of years.
שְׁתַּיִם is the feminine form of 'two' before the feminine שָׁנָה.
בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת is a merism: all further children, unnamed.
segments.note: Here the number is 'two and eighty' then 'seven hundreds'.

commentary.summary: Onkelos: 'after he begot Lamech seven hundred eighty-two years and begot sons and daughters', matching the English.

segments.english: All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years, and he died.
segments.literal: and-were all-of days-of Methuselah nine and-sixty year and-nine hundreds year and-he-died

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the verb is short (וַיָּמֹת) as is normal for the wayyiqtol of a hollow root

phrases.english: All the days of Methuselah were
phrases.literal: 'and-were all-of days-of Methuselah': a chain of constructs

grammar: כָּל־יְמֵי מְתוּשֶׁלַח is a construct chain: 'all the days of Methuselah'.
The verb וַיִּהְיוּ is plural although the sum of years is one figure: it agrees with 'days'.
וַיָּמֹת closes the entry with the formula of death; the silluq ends the verse and the ס marks a paragraph break.
segments.note: The total is the sum of 187 + 782 = 969 years.

commentary.summary: Onkelos: 'all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years, and he died', the same as the English.

segments.english: Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years, and he fathered a son.
segments.literal: and-lived-Lamech two and-eighty year and-hundred-of year and-he-fathered son

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of חיה; joined by maqqef to the subject

grammar: The pattern repeats from verse 25, with 'two' in place of 'seven'.
The zaqef gadol on לֶמֶךְ separates the subject from the figures.
בֵּן is indefinite: the unnamed son is named in the next verse.
segments.note: Rashi's midrashic remark on 'a son' is a homily, not a reading of the words.

commentary.summary: Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִבְנָה הָעוֹלָם, 'from him the world was built', a play on בֵּן and בנה. It is a homily and does not alter the plain sense.
Onkelos: Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years and begot a son, as in the English.

segments.english: He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands, from the ground that the LORD has cursed."
segments.literal: and-he-called [object-marker] name-his Noah saying this he-will-comfort-us from-work-our and-from-toil-of hands-our from-the-ground which cursed-it the-LORD

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of קרא; with 'name' it means 'to name'
נֹחַ; the explanation of the name is in the quoted words (root נוח 'rest', and נחם 'comfort')
לֵאמֹר, preposition ל with infinitive construct: introduces speech

tokens.gloss: he will bring relief to us
tokens.note: Piel imperfect with 1st plural suffix; Piel of נחם: 'comfort', here 'give relief'
Piel perfect with 3rd feminine singular suffix

phrases.english: This one will bring us relief
phrases.literal: 'this he-will-comfort-us': נחם 'comfort' taken in the sense of rest and relief following Rashi and Ibn Ezra

phrases.english: from our work and from the toil of our hands

grammar: The name נֹחַ is explained by wordplay with יְנַחֲמֵנוּ: the sounds נ-ח (root נוח 'rest', root נחם 'comfort') are close but not identical.
יְנַחֲמֵנוּ is Piel imperfect with the 1st plural suffix: 'he will comfort us'.
The gershayim and telisha gedola on זֶה mark a rare accent and give it weight at the opening of the quotation.
אֵרְרָהּ is a Piel perfect with a feminine suffix referring to הָאֲדָמָה; the antecedent is the ground, cursed in 3:17.
'The LORD' stands last in the verse, after the verb, with the silluq.
segments.note: The text itself says the name explains the saying; the pun is only approximate. The English 'bring us relief' follows Rashi (יָנַח, 'he will give rest') and Ibn Ezra (נחמה as rest from toil), who both read the name through נוח; the usual Piel sense 'comfort' (BDB) is kept in the gloss. The meaning of the name is kept out of the English line.

commentary.summary: Rashi: יָנַח מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת עִצְּבוֹן יָדֵינוּ, 'he will give rest from the toil of our hands'; before Noah they had no plough, and the earth gave thorns when they sowed wheat. Otherwise the wordplay on the name would fail and one would have to read his name מְנַחֵם.

Ibn Ezra: the sense is 'this one will give us rest (וננוח) from the toil of our hands'; Hebrew keeps the sense and not the exact words, as in יְרֻבַּעַל and יְרֻבֶּשֶׁת, and נֶחָמָה is rest from toil of the heart.
Radak: מִמַּעֲשֵׂנוּ means work of the ground, as in 'from his work from the field' (Judges 19:16).
Sforno: it is a prayer that this one comfort us by bringing rest from their work, since נֹחַ teaches rest, as in 'and rest from their enemies' (Esther 9:16).
Radak: Lamech did not speak by prophecy but gave the name as a sign, in blessing and prayer, as Rachel named Joseph; the English leaves it open as a statement of hope.

apparatus: Onkelos renders the verb with 'comfort' (יְנַחֲמִנָּנָא) and 'from our toil' (מֵעוֹבָדָנָא); 'מִלֵּאוּת יְדָנָא' for 'toil of our hands'.

segments.english: Lamech lived, after he fathered Noah, five hundred ninety-five years, and he fathered sons and daughters.
segments.literal: and-lived-Lamech after fathering-him [object-marker] Noah five and-ninety year and-five hundreds year and-he-fathered sons and-daughters
grammar: The structure is the same as verse 26, with Noah in place of Lamech.
חָמֵשׁ is the feminine form of 'five' with שָׁנָה; מֵאֹת is the plural of מֵאָה without the other long vowel.
The pashta on אַחֲרֵי and munaḥ on הוֹלִידוֹ show the temporal clause is one unit.
The revia on לֶמֶךְ marks the subject before the temporal clause.

commentary.summary: Onkelos: Lamech lived after he begot Noah five hundred ninety-five years and begot sons and daughters.

segments.english: All the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy-seven years, and he died.
segments.literal: and-were all-of days-of Lamech seven and-seventy year and-seven hundreds year and-he-died

phrases.english: All the days of Lamech were

grammar: The verse repeats the formula of 5:27 for Lamech.
The singular verb וַיְהִי (here) agrees with the sum as a whole, unlike the plural וַיִּהְיוּ in 5:27.
The total is 595 + 182 = 777 years.
The ס after the verse marks a paragraph break.

commentary.summary: Onkelos: all the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy-seven years, and he died.
